WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE

The purils of this excellent educational institution gave their annual entertainment at the Public Hall, on Thursday evening, under the presidency of the Mayor, when the youthful performers were honoured by an *audience which crowded the hall to its utmost capacity. Amonget the gentlemen present were—Alderman Holmes, Councillor Milner, Councillor Fell, Councillor 2.1.-,oks, Mr. C. Proadbent, J P., Mr. G. Artingetall, p , and Mr. W. Long, who are members of the school

committee, About 300 children were arranged on a raised platform. The girls, placed according to their years, were prettily attired in white, and their dresses were set cif with ribbons and rosettes of many colas rt, the juvenile assembly presenting both a grilling and brilliant appearance. In the musical por- tion of the entertainment the children, under the skilful leadership of Mr. Pattison, acquitted them- selves in a manner that elicited the hearty appreciation of the andience. Mr. Pattison, who has also achieved some distinction as a composer, included in the pro- gramme two of 'his own pieces—"A Venetian Boat Song" and" God Bless the Little Children." Both of them were capitally given, particularly the latter, Which is most expressive, and sung as it was by the chil- dren themselves, the effect was most touching. " The Three Little Pigs," a melody of an amusing characters was loudly encored, to which the children responded by singing "The Mermaid." The programme was full of exoellent pieces, which afforded the children full scope for a display of their abilities, and which were performed with perfect success. Mr. Twiss, the head master, and his numerous assistants were warmly complimented duritt the evening by the numerous friends of the institution upon the progress the pupils had evidently made under their tuition. In addition to the children's performance, Miss Mackereth, of Eccles, gave several of her readings, her rendering of a scene from the" School for Scandal," in which Sir Peter and Lady Teazle appear, obtaining marked approval. Mr. Stanley, of Bowdon, also gave a num- ber of tenor songs, and after the programme had been gone through, Mr. MILNEU then read the following report of the tesults of the examination for the year ending Septem- ber 30th, 1676, by her Majesty's Inspector of Schools, W. Scott C )ward, Lg. t—" The numbers have con- siderably increased here since my last visit, two years ago, and the schoolrooms seem to be as full as they should be, and to be incapable of accommodating any further increase. The state of efficiency attained is remarkable, and the school would now bear favourable comparison will any of its class whether as regards the high per °outage of passes or the excellent quality of the work done. I am especially struck with the grasp of the logical structure of the language which the parsing and analysis in the higher standards dis- play, and with the character of a large number of ex- ercises in composition, which showed that the minds of the writers had been trained to think and to express their thoughts with fair facility in words. The an- swering in reading gave good proof of similar careful and intelligent training. Throughout the Glasses a high standard is maintained successfully in every sub- ject. The drill, singing, and sewing are very credit- able, and the instruction of the pupil teachers is ex- cellent. The greatest credit is due to the devoted master, by whose zeal, intelligence, and tact, the school has reached its present stater" (Cheers.) 1 After reading the report Mr. Mireszn said: I have had a great many reports to read to you, and each re- port as it has come I have imagined to be as good as it was possible to be. This year, however, I think I have read to you the most satisfactory that it was ever my fortune to read. (Hear, hear.) Some of you who have been here in former years may remember that year by year we have promised increased teaching power and increased accommodation to keep pace with the continually increasing requirements of the Govern- ment code, but this report I think is a very fair reward for the efforts that have been made in this direction. Simply for this reason, the Government code some years ago simply required excellence is reading, writing, and arithmetic, and the efforts of the managers of the school have been to go somewhat beyond that, and to teach pupils committed to their care to think, and as the inspector says to express their thoughts with a fair amount of facility. I believe when this is attained a very large step has been made in the edu- cation of young people. (Hear, hear.) Last year the average attendance at school was 458. lam speaking now of the mixed school only, and not taking into oons sideration the infants' schools. The number actually examined by her Majesty's Inspector was 988, and out of these one-third were examined in the three highest standards, or rather more, the average number was 183. That is a very large per centage to present in these standards, and anon a per centage as very few schools can obtain. (Hear, hear.) In spite of the number who were examined in the higher standards there passed about e 3 per cent. (Hear, hear.) May I be allowed to mention a circumstance which has oc- curred recently, and which I think shows the success of the course of instruction carried' out in the school. rive of the prizes taken at the Grammar school the other day were taken by three boys, two of whom left our school at Christmas last, and the other only in April last. (Cheers.) The total number of prizes given at the Grammar School were 10, so that is one- sixth, and you must recollect we are only an elemen- tary school. (Cheers.) There is one thing which in- terferes with the amount of education that we should like to impart to the pupils, and that is the early age at which they have to leave school. The demand we have had for boys during the past t eelve months to supply the offices of the town has been more than we have been able to meet. Another subject I have to saention is that through the kindness of some ladies not connected with the school we are able to establish a cookery class. (Cheers.) It may seem an extraor- dinary thing to connect that with elementary educa- tion, but we believe it is one of the most important things in a girl's eduation, and although the class is only a small one at present, it may lead to something greater, and produce useful results. (Hear, hear.) Allow me on behalf cf the committee of this institu- tion to thank most cordially the parents of the children for the endeavours which we know they have made to ensure the regular attendance of the children, and last, but not least, to thank the pupil teachers and all who have had to do with the education of the pupils for the very earnest work they have given us during the past twelve months. (Losad cheer.) The MeTon said: I can assure you that the meeting this evening has been a source of gratification to my- pelf, and I am quite certain there is a great number of persons who have also been highly gratified with the proceedings this evening. (Hear, hear.) Fireeof all there are the parents of the children here—and I de- clare that I envy the parents of these children, and am sorry that I have no young children myself, to subject to the excellent teaching and discipline of the School. Then there are the teachers who must be greatly grafi- (tad to find that their efforts have been so well eecohded, and that their teaching as been so well re. eeived, and has resulted so satisfactorily. lam quite certain that to the teachers there is a great amount of credit due, and in this reaped I am irresistably carried back to former years, when such a sight as this would have gladdened the hearts of those who took a great interest in this School. The good Dr. Philip Carpen- ter—(cheers)— whom many of you may recollect as one who made vast efforts to establish, and found a task for music in the School, and whose efforts were

_ Incessantly directed towards that object—would have been delighted, could he have seen such a brilliant gathering as this, and have known that the seed he bad sown has been productive of such excellent results. (Cheers.) He is not present, but no doubt he will hear of it. and I am satisfied he will be delighted when he knows what satisfactory progress the pupils have made. In the days when he was connected with the

....___. . school, we were content with very humble results, and although he gave a great deal ot time to the work, it was not so well appreciated as it is now. To the com- mittee of the school it must also afford considerable

gratification' to find that their care and thought and the time which they have devoted towards the working out of their scheme of education, and adapting it to the school, has been attended with such successful results. (Gbeers.) I cannot help thinking that a great many of the parents who are outside, if they were only here listening to the beautiful eingiug of the children, and witnessing the effects of their attractive appearance, we should have no need of what is called compulsion. They would send their children to school without any Compulsion, as the beautiful sight before us would be sufficient to induce them to send their children to school, In order that they might become as proficient as the children now on the platform. (Cheers.) I cannot heipthinking that in some way or other the result of the to cert this evening will be tufficient to induce some (tort of the kind I have named. The music is delightiul, and Mr. Pattison must have spent many bottle in getting his young pupils to their present state of perfection, and to his teaching great credit is due. (Loud cheers.) it must 'shave been a source of anxiety to him in traMing them, and it must be a source of de- light to 11:m now to know how excellently they have seconded his efforts by acquitting themselves so satis- factorily. (Hear, hear.) I congratulate you and the children, and all connected with the school, on the As Mayor of the borough, I Success of this evening. feel a deep interest in an institution like this because I see in it the means ot elevating the ideas and opinions of those who will be the future men and women of the borough. (Hear, hear.) If they get Well trained in habits of thought, and receive a good sound education, they will be enabled to form a cor- rect opinion on public matters subroitted to them, and When they are trained to habits of order and discip- line, it will tend to make them good citizene of the borough, and good subjects of the Crown (Lond. cheers.) - -

Mr. Ammon/az said: Ladies and gentlemen, I have been requested to propose a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding this evening. I have great plea. sure in doing so, and also still greater pleasure in learning from the secretary that the parents of these children have assisted him in a great measure. It is complained in moat of the schools of the town that tl, . there is a difficulty in inducing parents to send their children to school, and if that difficulty were removed what a blessing it would be. (Hear, hear.) Thera 'I . never was a time in the history of this country when it odut tt ha • 17,701, hop th V•9l/14 theig4 In 141

leated than at the present day. I am glad that the Mayor has told me this evening that it is intended to make a movement in Warrington to put in operation a now Act of Parliament. I don't know exactly the modus operandi by which the Act will be worked, but if we can compel children to go to school and be edu- ceted, as these are now, the next generation will be much better than the pre, ent one. (Hear, hear.) We hear on all sides that the best sort of government is that where people govern themselves. That may be right in theory, but in order to make a government like that to work successfully, there must be some very important conditions. They must be taught to think, and to give a reason for whatever they do. (Hear, hear.) England has become a great nation, but it has not become great by being governed by an educated people. In ancient days this country was governed by a feudal aristocracy, and when that class became too selfish and indolent, it was succeeded by a parliamen- tary and constitntional government, in which V'e middle classes took a very important part. By their energy they brought about a very different state of things. They have encouraged industry in ovary I shape, and also established freedom of thought and speech in politics and religion. (Hear. hear.) The working classes at present form a vast majority in this country, and perform an important part in filling almost every electoral office; and in order that they should exercise their privileges aright, it is requisite that they should pass their time in an intelligent and rational manner. No one who has the least idea of human nature can for a moment suppose that we can all be of the same height, and there are quite as many I varieties of minds and dispositions as there are physical differences. It was ordained by Providence I that it should be so, but although there is this physical variety, yet we can become a happy and prosperous people. I believe the greatest enemy to the workiegman is he who ponders to his weakness. We hear a great deal of the rghts of workingmen, 1 but how can they enjoy their rights and privileges, unless you teach them to use that power aright by means of education, so that they may be a blessing to thetneolven and those around them. (Hear, hear.) Compare the man who goes home after his daily labour to his books and his family, to the man who goes to a public-house and there smokes and drinks,and you will find that the one has enjoyments which are great and ennobling,while the other is a specimen of human nature which is degrading and demoralising in its character and effects. I believe that no men are greater in mental energy than Englishmen, and they have power to become thoughtful, indwittious, and happy. There is nothing in this gauntry which cm present a working- man from becoming a gentleman in thought, manners,' and behaviour, honest and upright, and fearing no one. (Hear, hear.) It is the duty of everyone of us to do the best we can to promote the advancement of the people amongst whom we live, and the best thing we can do is to teach people not to depend on the rich, or the poor rates to assist them in sicknesses or old age, but to be independent by relying an their own exer- tions. (Cheers.) I have great pleasure now in thank- ing you for listening to me, and in proposing a vote of thanks to our worthy Mayor for presiding. (Cheers.)

Councillor MONIES seconded the vote of thanks, and remarked that the Committee was extremely anxious that the parents of the children should see that they were punctual and regular in their school attendance so that the efforts of the teachers might be supported to much as possible. Mr. Lozsa in supporting the resolution, expressed the Pleasure he had in being present, and said he felt sure the Mayor had never presided in his official capacity at any meeting with more pleasure than he did on that occasion.

M. TWIN, the head master, who was heartily re- ceived, said, when he was a pupil teacher in the old school, the Mayor was then one of the Committee, and he was also one of the oldest subscribers to the in- stitution. (Hear, hear.) His object in rising was to thank the parents for the great trouble they had taken in sending their children to the entertainment that evening in the manner they had done. (Hear, hear.)
The lavort briefly acknowledged the vote of thanks which was carried with acclamation, after which the proceedings were brought to a close.
GOOD TEMPLAR OF ENGLAND.

A session of the Good Templar Grand Lodge of Eng- land was held on Tuesday at Birmingham, over 600 members of the order being present. The Rev. Daw- son Burns, of London, read a paper on the Alpha Beta of the temperance question, arguing that the researches of chemistry, physiology, and psycology, proved that alcohol was a poison which affected every nerve and tissue of the body and mind. Alcohol a poison was the temperance Alpha; alcohol a brain poison, producing every species of vice and crime, was the temperance Beta. He urged closer attention to temperance educa- tion, and the bringing to this gpecial reform the plat- form, the press, the pulpit, and the poll.

div.head: HORRIBLE CRUELTY TO AN ASS.
div.p: HORRIBLE CRUELTY TO AN ASS.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Friday last, A man named Cartledge was summoned at the in. Stance of Inspector Carter, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, for cruelly treating a donkey. The Inspector stated that he found the donkey drawing a load of Bait, at midnight on the 4th inst. The animal was so weak that it had to be held up on each side by the defendant and his boy, and on releasing it from the cart the poor beast fell to the ground through exhaustion. It had no shoes on, it was lame on all four feet, and was covered with wounds. It was the practice in some parts of Lancashire to make donkeys work without ehoes,which was a source of great cruelty. On going to see the defendant next morning, he found he had had the donkey shoed, which must have caused it intense pain. Mr. Wall. veterinary surgeon, said the animal must have suffered moat excruciat,ox torture every time the nails were driven into its soft Loofa. Inspector Carter said he pressed for a heavy penalty, as the defendant was known to be very brutal towards his animals. The Mayor said it was the worst case they had ever had before them, and fined the defendant £6 and costs, or two months' imprisonment, with hard labour, in default.

div.p: MORRIBLE MURDER AT A BARRACKS.

On Christmas night a frightful scene was witnessed in the guardroom of Chelsea Barrack, where several of the men belonging to the Grenadier Guards were con- fined. One of these men, named ISPOonnor, as ailed another prisoner, named Johnson, as he lay on a bench, and killed him by repeated and violent kiclre on the head. When the murderer was arrested be appeared to be just recovering from a frenzy produced by drunkenness, and said he "didn't care at all."

div.head: BRAVE RESCUE OF A SINKING SHIP.
div.p: BRAVE RESCUE OF A SINKING SHIP.

A conspicuous act of bravery was performed by part of the crew of the steamer H. D. Pochin, which arrived at Falmouth on Monday. On Friday last, on perceiving a barque signalling that she was in a sink- ing state, there being a perfect hurricane and terrific sea, the second mate and six men volunteered to go in the lifeboat, in launching which there was great diffi- culty, and it was only after four hours that they could approach close enough to the barque to effect the res- cue of the poor fellows, some of whom were thrown overboard, but were saved by life bnoys.

WHAT CONSTITUTES "OFF THE PPEMISES." At the Warrington Police Court on Friday last, Albert Woods, a shopkeeper, of Bridge-street, holder of an exsise out-door license, was summoned for allowing beer to be drunk ou his premises. It was proved by Inspector Singleton and another officer that they found the baker and another man drinking in the defendant's bakehouse. Mr. Boyle, for the de- fence, contended that the bakehouse was not attached to the shop, _ and was not part of the premises for which the bowie was granted. The biker had sent for some beer for his breakfast, and merely gave his friend a drink for fetching it him. The Bench took a different view of the case, and inflict:3d a fine of 408. and note, and ordered the two men to pay costs for aiding and abetting.

ANOTHER DEATH IN THE HUNTING FIELD. On Saturday another ac'iident happened in the West Gloucestershire hunting field, and this time with a fatal termination. A horse ridden by Mr. John Rolt, of Ozleworth Park, in going at a fence stumbled and fell on his rider, rolling over him. Mr. Rolt was able to rise and walk with assistance a short distance to a neighbouring cottage. Here, however, he became worse, and he was at once removed to Berkeley Castle, where he shortly after died. Mr. Rolt was the eldest son of Sir John Rolt, who formerly represented Gloucestershire in the Conservative interest, and held high legal Office in the Conservative Government. The Berkeley hounds will not hunt again ,until after the funeral.

div.head: WANTED A SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WANTED A SCHOOL BOARD.

At the W'arringtoa Police Court, on Friday last, Three juveniles, said to belong to a gang of thieves, were brought up in custody and charged with stealing several articles from the various stalls in the market. The eldest prisoner, a boy of 16, named Gearing, stated he didn't know where he was born, nor who wore his parents; he had been in the Warrington Workhouse seven yea's, where he learned to read and write, but for the last few years he. had been trying to get his own living. For a fortnight he had not been in bed, having been sleeping in outhouses and at forges. He had no home, and was quite destitute. Mr. Broadbent remarked that it was high time there was a school board in Warrington, lo.r the Education Act put in force. The Mayor said something in that direction would be done shortly. Gearing was sent to an in• dustrial school for five years, and the other culprits were ordered to be whipped. MANCHESTER NONCONFORMITY.

The annual meeting of the Manchester Nonconformist Association was held on Friday, under the presidency of Mr. Joseph Leese. The Executive Committee re- ferred in their report to the success of the Govern. ment during the year in carrying measures which have a tendency to revive a system of sectarian education, hinder School Boards, and throw back the national system which had been partially inaugurated, and conk tended that this indicates the danger of national being sacrificed to party interests under a Conservative Government. Se long as the present reactionary Ministry continue in power, vigilance and effort will be needed on the part of Nonconformists and Liberals to oppose further retrogressive measures. The com- mittee urged Nonconformists to recngnise fully the sacred foundation on which their principles rest, and not to slacken their efforts till legislation is conformed to those principles. The report and statement of accounts were unanimously passed,and it was resolved, in accordance with the recommendation of the com- mittee, that the existence of other Nonconformist and Liberal organisations renders it necessary to continuo the more active operations of the association. A standing committee was therefore appointed to watch Nonoonformist interesta and take such action as may from time to time seem desirable.

Friday last was the prise day the Bandbach Grammar School. The Principal, the Rev. Mr. Mad. dock, presided, and he was supported by the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P. (who distributed the prizes), Mr. G. W. Latham, the Rev. T. C. Barker, late of christ Church College, Oxford, and the Rev. .T. Armit- stead, vicar of Sandbars's. There was .also present a large company of the• parents and friends of the pupils. The proceedings were of much interest. Mr. LATHAM, before making the presentation of the Latham Scholarship, said : In the first place he must disclaim all personal liberality a 9 far as that prize was concerned. Some kind friends were good enough to place a earn of money at his dispusal, to do what he liked with it. He felt that he could not do better with it than encourage what he had very mach at heart— the agricultural education-of farmers sons in Cheshire. He must say he rather hesitated as regards an obser- vation one often heard at meetings similar to the pre- sent, and that was these things were a great bless- ing and of great use to enable boys to rise gradually from one school to another, and to get, as it were, out of their own class and to become prodigies of learning. Much as he valued learning, and much as he liked to see se'f -taught men, yet, at the same time, he felt quite certain that that could not even be generally done. Life was too short, and they were all too busy, they had too much to do in this world of ours to enable very many of the clever ones to go out of the practical work of life and to take up learning for its own sake. There airway, would be some—they would have Fara- days in the school of science, they should have Tur- ners in the school of art who had risen from the very lowest ; but he, for himself, considered it far better, If they could somehow or other raise a man or a boy in his rank of life, and so raise his class with him. He thought there could be no happier a lot • for a youth than to attend a school of boys of his own rank, then to go out in the world and follow his father's profes- Mon, feeling at the same time that, by his conduct and knowledge, he was raising that profession. And another reason why he didn't so very much care about seeing learning pursued simply for its own sake, and boys stepping up to be men out of their own rank, was simply because such talent seldom con- tinued in a family. As agriculturists, they could en- sure by care in breeding the same excellence in generations of cattle and horses, and Mr. Darwin tld them that they could breed pigeons alike almost to a feather; but it was not so in intellect. There were two brilliant families in England—the Coleridges and the Wordsworths, but somehow it happened that their great men were either childless or left descendants very unworthy of them. He didn't know how it was, but it was so ; and therefore it seemed to him that talent among men hardly seemed to be inherited. He thought a man should work in his own class rather than try to get in a class very much obove him. This prize was given, not for any special knowledge, such as chemistry or botany, but for general culture. He made that condition, not bemuse he undervalued epeeial knowledge, but because he attached very groat importance to the general culture of farmers' sons in England. He was quite certain that if they were to raise their class they would never do it by cultivating special pursuits of a class but they would do it by putting into it something external. What Mr. Matt- hew Arnold gave as the definition of the Spirit of the Almighty, "Something not in us, but which tends to righteousness," was very applicable to what he believed tended to culture. AN ALTRINOHAM _BUILDER'S BANKRTJPTOY: A CURIOUS BUSINESS.

At a meeting of the creditors of Hr. S. P. Cardwell, builder, of Altrinoham, held at the Unicorn Hotel, Altrineham, in October last, and which was fully re- ported in the Mid-Cheshire Examiner at that time, it was resolved to make application .to the Registrar of the County Court to declare Mr. Cardwell a bankrupt. At the Manchester County Court, on Friday, this case came on for hearing on an application for him to be *declared a bankrupt. Mr. Smyley, instructed by Nicholls, Hinde, and Co., appeared for the petitioning creditor, and Mr. Atkinsoncrof Altrineham for a cre- ditor who holds a bill of sale on the property. The case on behalf of the petitioning creditor was that Cardwell was a trader until June last, whilst the case argued by Mr. Atkinson was that Cardwell ceased to be a trader un the 19th February last, since which time the business had been carried on by Mr. Joseph Gasgarth, of Altrinoham. John Brierley, of George. street, Altrinoham ; Mr. Thomas Dinning, of Broad- heath ; Thomas Boardman, formerly a foreman in the employ of Mr. Cardwell; Mr, Joseph B. Barrett, and Mr. J. M. Syers, accountant, of Altrinoham, gave evi- dence on behalf of the creditor. Mr. Syers stated that he was appointed receiver under Mr. Cardwell's room. position in June, 1875, and he afterwards made out the promissory notes. The first of notes became due on the 19th October, 1875. Since the 22nd June this year he had been to Mr. Cardwell's late place of busi- ness three or four times, but he had not been able to find him. He had also instituted inquiries at Mac- clesfiel t, Alderley Edge, Morecambe, Southport, and various other places where he had been told he was, but without success. He had done his best to find him, but had failed. Cross-examined I believe you are one of the principal instigators of these proceedings P I am. And you called a meeting, I think P I did. I believe it is the result of your endeavour that these proceedings are brought about P I failed in my first attempt, but I succeeded in this. You could not find anyone who would present a petition, I suppose P No. the party who was to assist me, I suspect was paid to get out of the way, but I don't know by whom. You could not find one creditor who would be silly enough to present a petition P Mr. Smyly: We will sea whether it is silly or not. Witness (to Mr. Atkinson) At the time of the meeting that was held at Altrincham, I thought Mr. Cardwell was dead. I was afterwards told that he was likely to be indicted for felony. Don't you think that was the reason why he went away? I cannot tell. I don't think ,it was the sole reason, by any means. Do you believe it was an inducement for him to go P I cannot say. To the Registrar: I had great reason to suspect that the transaction looked black, and in consequence I willed a meeting of credi- tors at Altrincham, to see if we could not get Mr. Cardwell made a bankrupt. To Mr. A•kinson To some extent I called that meeting in justification of myself. At that meeting I expressed an opinion that Cardwell was dead. After that meet- ing, a legal friend of mine said, " Teere are good logi- cal reasons why he is out of the way." I said," What are they P" and he told me. What were the" good logical reasons "that your legal friend told you ? To get out of the way of this felony, and other pressure. That meeting took place at the end of October P I dare say it would be about that time. And down to this petition being presented in December you were not able to induce anyone to present a petition ? At that meeting it was agreed that a party named Taylor should join me in petitioning this court, and a Mr. Dixon was to meet me on the Thursday to arrange what should be done. I wrote to him to keep his ap- pointment, but he did not do so. He must have passed my office and gone to the office of another party, and I have great reason to say, to use classical language, that he was made a " sucking dove" of. (Laughter.) Mr. Smyly: And en it rolls. (Laughter.) Witness: Well that was the language of Mr. Atkinson's client. Mr. Gaskarta told me himself that he had made him into a sucking dove. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Attkin- son : They did not try to make a sucking dove of you? No, nor I don't -think you will. (Laughter.) You are not so easily smoothed over? No; I am rather rough in the bristles. (Much laughter.) When you failed to get this sucking dove to present a petition you looked out for another? I did. Who is paying the costs of these proceedings? Are you doing something towards it? To tell the truth I am. Who else?. The creditors have promised, and I have no doubt they will do it. I suppose you are giring all the instructions? lam doing my best. And you are paymaster, I suppose ? No. The Registrar: Do I understand that all the creditors at that meeting have promised to pay? Witness: They promised to sub- scribe to carry this out. Mr. Attkinson : How many of the creditors? Witness I think there was 28. I Have they all signed a memorandum to pay their share of the expense P No; it was carried by resolu- tion, But you know that you should get something better than a mere resolution. Unfortunately, I have trusted human nature too much to take care of myself. (Laughter.) You don't mean to try sucking doves any more ? (Laughter.) My confidence in honest human nature is not yet shaken. (Laughter.) Mr. Spryly: The creditors came to the conclusion that this was a gross swindle, and they subscribed the money? They said they would. Have you advanced money becaase it is a gross swindle? Yee. You believe it is a gross swindle? I do. I have done the beat I could to find Cardwell. His wife does not know anything about his being dead. I think his being dead is a "put up." Mr. Gaakarth told me he had met Dixon at the end of last year or the beginning of this. Mr. Smyly submitted that he had fully established his Case. Ur. Atkinson stated that at the end of Fohruary Mr. Cardwell ceased to lee a trader. Prior to his failure in 1875, he carried on the business of builder, and when he effected the composition, like many men did, he undertook to pay more than he was in a position to do. He afterwards endeavoured to carry on his business, but towards the end of the year, when the payments under the composition began to fall due, it became evident that it was perfectly impossible for him to continue to carry on his business, the consequence being that on the 19th of February, in this year, he entered into an arrangement with Mr. Gaskarth to continue to work for him, but in the capacity of a servant. From that date he became servant to Mr. Gaskarth, who paid him £2 a week wages, and also paid all that was expended for building purposes. He should be able to prove that from the 19th February Mr. Cardwell had not bought or sold a single thing for the purpose of trade on his own account; but that by the arrangement which was made Mr. Gaskarth found the money for the settlement of bills and for payment of the wages. It might be that Mr. Cardwell never told the workmen of the change ' • it was not likely that he would, and he (Mr. Atkinson) did not think it was an advisable thing to do. It was perfectly immaterial to the men from whom they received their money. He called Mr. Edward Nall, who stated, I am a book- keeper, and am on the premises that were formerly Mr. Cardwell's. I was with Mr. Cardwell prior to February last, when there was a change. Mr. Card- well told me that Mr. Gaskarth was to find all the money for every transaction from the 19th February, and that he was to receive £2 a week as wages. After that arrangement Mr. Gaskarth found the money for the wages. After Mr. Cardwell went away, the business proceeded in precisely the same manner. The account produced is one rendered by Mr. Cardwell to Mr. Gaskarth, and it contains one item of £2 10s., 'wages and expenses'' due to Mr. Cardwell himself. By Mr. Smyly—Nobody knew that but yourself. And Mr. Cardwell. I have no cottages belonging to Mr. Cardwell in my possession. They belonged to him at one time, but I paid him for them. I cannot tell when I paid him. It was in 1874 when I paid the deposit. Cardwell has not been near the place that I know of since the 21st June. I have been there all the time. I did not know he was going. He went away sud- denly. Ihe Registrar said that unless Mr. Atkinson bad evidence that would carry his ease further he thought he had no chance of success. Mr. Atkinson said that after that expression of opinion he should not call further witnesses. The Registrar signed the usual form adjudicating Mr. J. P. Uardwell, a bankrupt.

FREEHOLDERS.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board with regard to the land required by the Board from the Kuutsford freeholders to erect a new hospital Upon. The Local Government Board says that the Guardians propose to purchase land from a number of persons described as freeholders, the consideration being a perpetual rent; but the Board are unable to satisfy themselves as to the title of these persons to make such a conveyance. The freeholders are in any place not a corporate body competent to hold land or to make any conveyance, and the gentlemen who are named on the draft are not joint tenants holding the , land in any joint right, and are therefore not capable of making a grant of the land in fee simple. The Workhouse was built in 1833, upon a piece of land described as part of the waste or common in Little Kuutsford, and that piece of land was enclosed from the common under the provisions contained in the Act of George 111., 22, and rendered applicable to the unions formed under the 4th and sth William IV., c. 76, by the sth and 6th William IV., c. 69. By the , instrument then executed the Lord of the Manor and the major part in value of the freeholders and com- moners gave their consent thereto gratuitously. The Board do not think it was intended that the consent should be subject of bargain, and sale, and the statute does not provide any means by which the purchase money should be estimated and paid. The Board Bug- gestea that the course adopted at the time of the .erection of the Workhouse should be repeated. The Board suggest that the Lord of the Manor as owner of the land subject to the rights of common, will sell his interest therein, 'and several commoners will dispose of their rights in the same. In such a case the Guar- dians must ascertain the total sum payable to each person accor ling to his interest. The stipulations which propose to bind the Guardians in their future action are likewise open to great objection, as if it were en- tered into they may seriously hamper the Guardians hereafter. The CLERK characterised some of the poarts of the letter as being absurd, and maintained the action of the Guardians and the decision of the freeholders to be in every way correct, and instanced cases of persons purchases in Knutsford. The applicant was a boatman named Thomas Carrington, who informed the police that when at Leigh, a few days ago, another boatman named John Taylor offered to sill him the woman with whom he was living, named Sarah Tyrer. The woman, who was present, said "Aye do sell me, he has been wanting to live with me a good while," but Taylor finding Carri ,gton eager for the purchase increased his price to 17s. 6d. div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOE NOTT, OF KNIITSFORD.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOE NOTT, OF KNIITSFORD.

Many of the inhabitants of Knutsford will learn With regret of the death of Mr. Joe Nott, of the Firs, Over Knutsford, which took place on Friday last. The deceased, who was 27 years of age, was the eldest son of the late Mr. Joe Nott, of Fallowfleld, near Man- chester, who was in business in that town as an oil and tallow merchant up to the time of his death, which took place some four or five years ago. At the time of the father's death the widow with her two eons, Harry and Joe, came to reside at the Firs, Kuutsford. These two young gentlemen, being engaged in no _business, had.opportunittes of going about the country and making acquaintances and friends in a manner that is not possible by people engaged in the ordinary pursuits of business. They were more widely known and more popular than perhaps any other two young gentlemen of the county. The high good humour, wit, and generosity of the deceased endeared him to all with whom he came in contact, and made him a genial friend mid jovial companion. The funeral took place on Wednesday, at Ardwiek Cemetery, Manchester. As the funeral cortege—which consisted of a hearse, a mourning coach, and the private carriage of the family—passed, the inhabitants of the town had their blinds drawn, as a mark of respect to the memory of the deceased. The death of Mr. Nott is rendered ad- ditionally painful from the fact that he was to have been married in a few weeks.—Cont.

Marshall, Mr. Isaac Speakman, and Mr. Andrew Brown, three of the leading ettemist3 in Run- corn, were summoned for selling to Superintendent Steen, two ounces of milk of sulphur, the same not being of the nature, substance, and quality of the article demanded.—Mr. Henry Glaisyer, LL.B., of Birmingham, instructed by the Chemists and Druggists Trade Association, defended in all the oases. In cross-examinetion by Mr. Glaisyer, Dr. Bell said that milk of sulphur, prepared so as to con- tain sulphate of lime, was an adulterated article, on the ground that it contained a foreign ingredient, which was not pure sulphur,—For the defence. He also showed that milk of sulphur was preferred to eulph. pmcip. on account of the former containing sulphate of lime; and in sup- port of this two wholesale druggists of Liverpool were called, who showed that thirteen times as much milk of sulphur was sold as the other preparation. Dr. Oliver Pemberton of Birmingham, professor of surgery to the Birmingham College, said he had been in practice thirty years and had never heard of milk of sulphur being injurious to anyone ; on the contrary, 1 it was more beneficial than precipitated sulphur, mad was much more palatable to patients. THE BOARD AND RELICUOITS OBSER. VA NOES.

Mr. Thom, the chairman, called attention to the desirability of opening the board schools with singing and prayer. His feeling was that some sort of hymns and prayers should be used which had no distinctively dogmatic teaching. The board might not agree as to creeds, but the great truths of Christianity they all believed, and unless some sort of religious instruction was given in the school many children would go with. out it through either the neglect or incompetence of their parents. Originally, he was an advocate of secular teaching, but now he did not think it desirable, and be went in heartily for religious instruction, viz , the broad truths of Christianity without any dogmatic teaching. If that course were adopted general atis. faction would be given to the ratepayers, as he believed the inhabitants of the town were decidedly against the board schools becoming secular schools. From eleven school boards returns had been received in favour of religious observance at the opening of the school. viz.. Louden; Sheffield, Huddersfield, Sunderland, New. castle-on-Tyne, Liverpool, Blanchester, Hull, Leeds, Leicester, and Nottingham. The Liverpool prayer book was decidedly the best, composed as it was of collects of the Church of England, and included some of the most beautiful prayers ever written by the fathers of the Church. They cou. tamed nothing destruetive or dogmatic, nor anything that would give offence to the most tender conscience. This book had been in use in the temporary schools of the Board, and he begged to move that the schools be opened with singing and prayer, and that the prayers be the same as used hitherto, with the addition that the Lord's Prayer be printed on the fret page for daily MO.

It was a most praiseworthy thing that these men ehould devote their energies on Sundays to the religious education of the young, after they had been hard at work all the week, and he held that the work these men did on Sundays exceeded by far their weekly labours. They must also remember that their teachers: and superintendents laboured there without any reward in the shao of money. The only reward they had was the satisfaction of knowing that they were doing good, and that they were training the children in that part of Warrington in the paths of virtue and religion. They might not live to see the fruits of the education which was given there, but some day no doubt others would see it ; and he was persuaded that the neighbourhood of Bank Quay was vastly im- proved during the five years that eahool had been in existence. It was perfectly certain that every good man who laboured in that school was a centre of geed jut:Bianca to those around him; and as many in that neighbourhood formerly spent some part of Sun- day in the public-house, now they would not be seen there on any account whatever. (Hear, hear.) Such a change was gratifying, the only difficulty was that the schoolroom was not large enough, and the children were too many. He was told by the euperintdente that they really felt it would be a relief if the numbers were somewhat diminished by the new schocl which had been opened at Sankey Bridges, because there were too many children for the size of the school to manage it properly. He could not sit down with- out adding his expression of regret and sorrow at the loss they had sustained by the aeath of their friend, Mr. Clough. (Hear, hear.) He believed every child in the school was food of Mr. Clough who had the power of attracting everybody to him by his geniality. He understood that at his funeral some hundreds of persons were present, and the greatest respect was shown to his memory. That spoke a great deal for a man in very humble circumstances, who never was more than a labouring man, and yet who weilded such a powerful Influence for good. (Hear, hear.) The annual tea party and ball in connection with the Olive Branch Lodge, No. 1,120, was held on Tuesday evening last, at the house of Bro. Edward Badley, Unicorn lan, Winwick-street, when upwards of sixty members and their friend sat down to a sub. stantial knife and fork tea, provided by the host and hostess. Mather, who an- nounced that the Warrington district was in a flourish- ing condition both financially and numerically. A WORKINGMAN AND MUNICIPAL PURCHASES.

A meeting of working men and others was hell in the Cairo-t. Schoolroom, Warrington, on Thursday, to hear an address by Mr. Diggle on the Gas Works purchase. Mr. Diggle, a Warrington working mao, who it will be iemembered some time since desounced, in a public lecture in the same room, the convict Richard Banner Oakley and his Co-operative Credit Bank swindle, and whose shrewd and humorous observations on public: affairs always prove attractive and entertaining, ex- plained at considerable length his views on the Gas purchase question. The room was crowded. In front of the platform were placed copies of posters contain- ing the names of " a few of the multitude who are in favour of the Gas purchase." The audience seemed equally prepared for instruction or merriment. The lecturer, a grizzled, elderly man, who has evidently been a hard worker in his time, disdained the fashion- able habiliments of the popular lecturer, and, like the late Lord Grey, seethed "resolved to stand by his order," and wore the blue sin ock in which he earns a lab°. rims and honourable livelihood. The lecture possessed many points of interest, and was frequently remark. able fee the hard-headed common sense for which men like Mr. Diggle are often distinguished. Perhaps it wanted coherence, and that literary symmetry which are not always commanded even by those who have leisure, and have had the advantages of systematic culture, Mr. Diggle's audience was good humoured throughout, unless one might coustrue to the contrary their frequent jocular interpolations. The report of such a lecture is necessarily fragmentary, but amongst other things Mr. Diggle said that in the matter °lithe Co-operative Credit Bank they found he was right, and they would find him right now. (Hear, hear.) He should submit teethe meeting 13 reasons why the town should purchase the Gas Works, and after he had done so, he should be glad to answer any questions, and permit a discussion on the subject. (Applause.) He thought that they, as the ratepayers i of Warrington, should be not only n possession of the Gas Works but also of the Water Works. (Cheers.) He had always been in favour of that, and coming from Manchester, he knew of the great advantage to that town that the Gas and Water Works had been. (Hear, hear.) The last year he was it Manchester, the profits derived from the Manchester Gas Works were £63,010, and last year, he had no hesitaion in saying, they were £lOO,OOO. That was something worthy of consideration. (Applause.) Those profits were ap- plied to the town's improvements, and contribued very considerably to the improvement rate. They (the Core poration of Warrington) had to keep the streets le repair, which, with the present system of rock founds. tions and other improvements, rendered them very expensive. (Hear, hear.) Therefore they should not be disturbed if it could be possibly avoided when once well laid down, as they could not be made the same again if interfered wita either by the insertion of gas or water pipes. (Cheers.) After epeaking of the time the questioa had occupied in the Council, he said that they appointed the Council to manage their affairs—of course it was their House of Parliament, with great I power. The 36 gentlemen of which it was composed I had great interest in the town, and he (the lecturer) had great confidence in them. They had the interest of the town at heart, and had individually a great in. terest at stake, therefore they would look after what was really their own interest. (Hear, hear.) He Wee very sorry to say that the Town Council—by those who sent them there' the working classes—had not had the deference paid to them due to their judgment and ex. perience. Some persons looked upon them as if they were taking something from them, the consequence of which would be, in his opinion, that nobody of honour and character would care to go into the Council, but would prefer to mind their own prieate businesses. (Hear, hear.) The Council appointed certain gentle. men to negotiate for the purchase of the leas Werke, and they had great difficulties to contend with. Let them jest see who those gentlemen were. There was Mr. Beamont, a lawyer of some standing, who had gone through some service, who had not retired on half but full pay. (Laughter.) He had done well for himself and for Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Then there was Mr. Fell, a gentleman well known in connection with Parr's Bank and the Bewsey Forge. He was a man of vigour and integrity a quaker, and they generally understood a thing or two. (Laughter.) Another was Ald. Chas. Holmes, also a member of the Society of Friends (they were all of a good stamp) although he did not know mach about him. (Laughter.) The next and most impore tent and most abused was Aid. Davies. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Not being a Warringteuian he did not know how he had got up to his present position, but he saw that he was an accountant by profession. They, the accountants, had an association or Trades' Union, which held its meetings in London, of which Ald. Davies had been Chairman since its beginning, up to the present time. (Hear, hear.) That ehewed that somebody thought something of him, whether they did or not. (Laughter.) Of the gas dir. eters he would say he only wished that he was one. (Laughter.) Had anybody except those interested in the gas works, approached them, they would not have been received, but would have been shown the door. (Laughter.) The difficulties in negotiating a matter of that kind were greater than those in any ordinary affair, be. cause they were getting as much as it was proposed to give them, or something more. (A voice, let them keep it.) The directors had .6600 a year, and two of those gentlemen war getting more from their office as directors, th from their shares held by them. Now Mr. Brown how do you manage that. (Laughter.) In speaking of the light duties of the directors, he said teat after die. posing of the coal contracts, tec., they simply met to have a bit of chat, and got two guineas when they had done. (Laughter.) The two gentlemen he had re. ferred to, when the matter came forward to be decided, had the power of stopping the sale, having as many proxies in their pockets as would enable them to do so. Well, now, what do you think about that? (Hear, hear.) (A Voice ' It's a shame. We've head that before, lair. Diggle.") Mr. Diggle: Well, you have heard it again. RE-ASSEMBLING OF
CONFERENCE.:

The re-assembling of the Conference, which took place on Thursday, is expected to have important results, although it seems probable that its deliberations may be re- sumed on Saturday. According to advices from Constantinople it appears to be certain that the Porte will not absolutely reject the proposals of the Towers, but erely raise objections on certain points. The Turkish. war party is said to be somewhat strong. but a peaceful solution is not considere,i impos- sible. Moreover, if the principles laid (lowa by the Powers be maintained, the Pleni- potentiaries appear disposed, it is declared, to discuss the details. In the event of war, it is stated that the Porte will arm at Con- stantinople forty battalions of Nationt,l Guards, comprising men of various religions. One thing is perfectly clear. The Powers are quite agreed as to the nature of the de- mands to be submitted to the Porte The wicked and incessant efforts made in this country by certain portions oft e Conserva- tive press to excite jealousy of Russia have resulted in a perfect accord between Lord Salisbury and the Russian representative at Constantinople. The Powers will accept no idle promises of amendment from Turkey, but will certainly insist on material guaran- tees such as must satisfy those who find it impossible to have faith in the falsest Go- vernment in Europe. The Times is of opinion that "The more fanatical of the Turks may be ready to risk a war rather than undergo such a humiliation; but it is difficult to believe that Midhat Pasha would be so infatuated. Having some knowledge of Eu ope, he must be aware that the contest would be a fight, not for Bulgaria, but for the very existence of the Porte. 13, may pardonably have been hopeful so long as the Great Powers seemed to be at variance, aud he would not have been a Turk if he had not tried to disunite

them by menaces. But so intelligent a man must have seen the folly of open defiance when Lord Salisbury and General Ignatieff cordially agreed to recommend the same propositions. If he should still refuse to be guided by the Conference, the reason must be that; he fears to break with the proud and am bitious party which has raised him tn the Grand Vizierate."

On Friday the German Parliament was closed by the Emperor William. In the Speech from the Throne His Majesty referred with gratification to the measnres that had been passed, especially those which would assist in effecting the legal unity of the country. He hoped that when the members mat again they would be able to direct their excluaive attention to this sub. Pict. With regard to the Eastern Question, the Eoipzor said that the negotiations, as far as they had id herto proceeded, justified the hope that his !Tor's, and the conciliatory and peaceful intentions of the Powers im- mediately concerned, would successfully solve pending questions, without prejudice to the good relations now existing. Germany would continue, by friendly and disinterested mediation, to lend co-operation for the attainment of this end.

MURDEROUS ATTACK ON AN ALTRINOHAM GAMEKEEPER.

Charles Leyland and Ralph Leyland, 3 Antos, of Altrincham, were charged, on Wednesday, at the Altrincham Police Court, with unlawfully wounding Wm. Ashley, gamekeeper, on the previous night, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. P.C. Roscoe stated that he was on duty at Oldtield, Altrincham, when he heard cries of " Murder " pr-ceed from Mr. Ashley's house. He ran there, and on entering the yard he apprehended the two prisoners, who were making off. On entering the house, he found Mr. Ashley covered with blood, lying on the sofa. He was unable to speak, but the constable was told by his wife and daughter that the prisoners had caused the injuries to his head, lie found the prisoners' hats on the table. Dr. Blease said that the wound on the head was some six or eight inches in length, and per e- trated to the bone. The wound was of an excessively dangerous character, and, under the most satisfactory circumstances, it would be at least ten days before prosecutor could appear to give evidence. The pri- soners were remanded until Wednesday. next. Mr. Norris said that they might pray daily and fervently to God that the prosecutor might recover, as should he not do, they would be placed in a deplorable posi- tion. The prisoners stated that they were attacked by prosecutor's son and several others, seho had illtreated and knocked down Charles, and they escaped from them. On passing Oldfield Hall they heard their pur- suers, by whom they were overtaken and beaten. They went into Ashley's house to complain of his son's conduct, when he attacked them with an iron scraper.

div.head: CHURCH RATES IN CHESHIRE,
div.p: CHURCH RATES IN CHESHIRE,
THE RIVER 'WEAVER FUND.

Tun days of Church rates are past and gone. It has been settled by the Legislature that any taxation of the people in general for the support of the Churches a one privileged sect, is illegal, and that only in cases where money borrowed in the old times has not yet been repaid, or where the rate has been sub- stituted by Act of Parliament for tithes, shall any further collection of rates be made. The spirit of the age has brought about this result. It is a natural corollary of all the great measures for the ielief of Noncon- formists from pains and penalties which have been passed in spite of Tory growls and grumblings. It is consistent Nele% the spirit—if not with the:practical working out —of the conscience clauses in the Education Act.

But in this county of ours there is going to be made an attempt to revive Church rates uuder a new form. Our readers may remember that some thirty-five years ago the Trustees of the River Weaver obtained power from Parliament to build three churches, at Winsford, Northwich, and Weston Point, to endow them when built, and to devote a specified sum to their repair from time to time. As the revenues of the river belong after the payment of the neces- sary cost of repair and maintenance to the ratepayers of the cou.ty, and any decrease of the net revenue implies an increase in the rates of the county, these churches were practically built at the expense of the rate- payers, who, therefore, whether Noncon- formists or Church of England, were forced to contribute to the erection of these State churches. Of course, even so long ago, the matter was strongly fought, but the prin- ciple ot the abolition of Church rates was not then firmly established, and Parliament in its wisdom saddled the ,ratepayers of the county with an annual charge for churches, denominational schools, and repairs to the tune of some £5OO per annum, besides the deduction of the money necessary to build the original structures. That, however, is past and gone. It is no good crying for spilt milk. All we can do is to wipe up the mess, and try to stop the same carelessness and stupidity again. But now a new attempt at injustice is gethag to be made. One of these churches is gradually, from the sinking of the ground, going to decay. We take a special interest in its tumbling condition, for it seems to us to be a type of the whole State Establishment which from the rottenness of its foundation, and the gradual decay going on inside it, is also rapidly going to pieces, and after all we shall not be surprised if the Church at Wins- ford lasted as long as the State Church of England. The Trustees of the River Weaver, however, purpose in a bill which they have just deposited in the Houses of Parliament, to take power to remove this tumbling edi- fice, to re-build it in a safer place, and so to perpetuate the injustice. Time, it is said, is on the side of the party of progress, but in this case that proverb is baffled an set at naught by succeeding generations of Tory Cheshire Squires, who, in the interest of the sect to which most of them belong, repair the ravages of time, and in 1877 hope to do unopposed what was thought to be objectionable in the darker times of Church privilege and supremacy. It must be remembered that every shil- ling spent on this proposed rebuilding is so much taken from the sum to be given in aid of the county rates. True it is that we re- ceive little from the river now, and are likely to receive less in future, bat that has arisen from what we believe to have been an honest though ill-considered attempt on the part of the trustees to adapt their river to the exigencies of the salt trade and to meet the competition of the railways. But a time must come when the debt incurred for these purposes will have been discharged and pctyment to the County Treasurer resumed. A delay of a simple day in this resumption of payment, the abstraction of a single shilling for denominational purposes willbe in our opinion a fraud on the general body of , ratepayers in the county, and we trust that steps will betaken at once to oppose the ob- jectionable clauses before the committee of , each house of Parliament.

Without doubt the majority of the trustees put their trust in the Conservative brute force which, at the present moment, over- bears all fairness and honesty in the settle- ment of such questions. After the sad experience at the end of the last session of how a measure may be worked in the interests of a denomination, we are inclined to believe that they are right enough in thinking that the House of Commons as a body are capable of assenting to any job whereby the powers of the Church of Eng- land may be sustained for a few years longer. But in this case the matter has to go before an independent committee, to be argued by counsel, and to be supported by witnesses. The committee is more in the nature of a Court of Justice than of a legis- lative—and consequently a prejudiced,— assembly. It is possible, therefore, that jus- tice may te done, and that this attempt by a private bill to do what has been declared by a public one no longer legal, will signally fail. But however that may be, we are sure that the attempt to use public money for semi- private purposes will neither be forgotten nor forgiven soon. These self-elected Trustees, who have by this proposal proved that they was incapable of understanding the national feeling by which Church rates were abolished, who have, shown 'themselves in- sensible to the claims of justice, must be replaced by others who being elected by the ratepayers, will be answerable to their con- stituents for their conduct. Doubtless all these gentlemen are in their private capacity honourable men, even if in most cases they are not business men, and utterly in- competent to manage a great trading con- cern. They would shrink from applying a single farthing entrusted to them for one purpose, for a totally different one, without the leave of thq donor. They would con- eider it as a miserable subterfuge, if they ap- plied for a private Act of Parliament, to enable them as .:- ndividuals, to set aside the 'wishes of a body of subscribers to some special object. But the misfortune is that men who are of the strictest probity when WWI; fin themeolygo pi% 19 W 4 pi to

feeling of responsibility, when they, meet as a public body. The history of all our Charities and Endowments proves this. It is the practice now in all new schemes for Charities to take away the power of co- option from the Trustees, and to make them representatives of some interest, which is concerned in the Charity. As the Weaver Trustees are applying for a new Act, we trust that they will consider whether they might not include among its clauses some plan by which the body might be represen- tative of the ratepayers, and add to the benefits they have bestowed alreasly on their county the one most inestimable one of " the happy despatch."

The following letter has been received from Mr. John Bright :—" Rochdale, 26th December, 1876.— Dear sir,—You have sent me a report of a speech by Mr. Hick, M.P. fox Bolton. He makes no Attempt to answar anything I have said, but contents himself and hie audience with such misrepresentation of me as may be picked up in the c.olumns or the gutters of his party. The two things he affirms of me are entirely false, as he must have kt. own if he has read the speech to which he refers. If he has not read it, it would have been better of him to have said nothing about it. It is curious to observe how exactly the speeches of Tory members are adjusted to the ignorance and passion of those whom they address. It may be the natural level of the speakers; if not, they succeed in reaching it without diffionity, and once at that level they seers incapable of rising above it. Thank you for sending me the newspaper, and I am very respectfully yours. Joins BI T.—Mr. Edward Guy, 17, Church-street, Leigh.

A CHRISTMAS GIFT TO EARL GROBVEROB.—The Countess Grosvenor was safely delivered of a daughter on Christmas eve at Saighton Grange, the reridence of the earl and countess. Both mother and child are doing well. The Duchess of Westminster was at Saigh- ton during the evening. - - - -
ALrianicmat _Poo= COMIT.—On Wednesday James Hankiason, labourer, Altrineham, was fined 64. and ss. 4d. costs for being drunk and riotous in Sandiway, Altrmoham, on the previous night.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT ALTRINCIIAN —The annual tea party of the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the New-street School-room on Christmas day. As usual there was a large attendance. Tho speeches were interspersed with singing and mita- tions.

THE LATE CURATE OF CABEINCITON.--A purse of £26 was the other day presented to the Rev. R. Bramley, late curate of Carrington, by some of his clerical friends in Manchester, as some token of sympathy with him in the circumstances under which he was compelled to leave the neighbourhood.

NORTHWIOEL WESLEYAN CnsPEL ANNIVERSANY.— On Sunday last two sermons wero preached, morning and evening, in the Wesleyan Chapel, Leftwich, by the Rev. W. Gooderidge, of Manchester. Collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the trust fund, which realised about £l2. MURDER OF A SON IT BOLLINOTON.—Mr. Robt. Hal- liwell, rope manufacturer, Bollington, was committed for trial on Tuesday for the murder of his son, a lad of 13. Mr. Halliwell, who had been pronounced in- sane, strangled the boy" to put him out of misery," the unfortunate man being under the delusion that hie family would come to poverty. Tax WorirmErar, Wsratun, WESTON.—Weston has failed to accomplish the task begun by him at the Agricultural Hall, London, last Monday, of walking 605 miles in six days. After having walked over 460 miles of ground and one lay, he retired between eleven and twelve o'clock on Saturday night, leaving 45 miles to be traversed to complete the journey. WHISKEY SHEIGOLINGIN SCOTLAND:A few days ago an Inland Revenue officer and a preventive man dis- covered an illicit whiskey-still among the hills above Port Lair, near the entrance to Lock Torridon. Hav- ing destroyed the materials, they apprehended two men in the " bothy," but near Inveralligin they were met by a crowd of villagers, who rescued the smugglers and maltreated the excisemen. A CHEWIER CONSTABLE DESERTING TO THE ARMY: At Macclesfield, on TUesday, Edward Hindley, an officer in the Cheshire County Constabulary, was fined £2 and costs, or two months' imprisonment, for deser- ' ting from his post without giving notive previous to leaving the village (Millington) where he was sta- tioned. He had a quarrel with his wife, and after- wards joined the Royal Attillery, from which he had since deserted and surrendered to the police. Ile ws remanded on the charge of desertion. WESLEYAN SUNTAN' SCHOOL NOBTHWICEL On Christmas Day the seventh annual social tea meeting was held in the Leicester-street schoolroom, when about 300 persons partook of tea. The same evening a public meeting was held, when a selection of music, recitations, singing, readings, speeches, &c., were given by the teachers and scholars. The Rev. A. Burgess occupied the chair. A collection was made at the close which, together with the proceeds of the tea meeting, realised about £l2.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO AN EXPRESS TRAIN. —A. disastrous railway accident occurred on the Great Northern Railway at Arlesey station, five miles from Hitohin, on Saturday afternoon. When the Manches- ter express, from King's Cross at 2-45, reached that place it ran into a goods train which was being shunted. The express was proceeding at the rate of forty ini,.es an hour at the time, and aix of the carriages were greatly damaged. The driver and stoker of the express and three passengers were killed, while about thirty passengers were injured, some of them seriously. BOBBING Tali DEIN Or OBEBTBB'e HENBOOBT.—On Friday, William Sharpe was brought up before the city magistrates at Chester, charged with breaking into the premises of the Dean of Chester, also with violently assaulting Police-officer Snaith. Between one and two o'clock on Sunday morning, the officer was on duty near King Charles's tower, City Walls and met a man carrying some fowls. The officer at- tempted to arrest him, when a struggle ensued. The man struck the officer. a violent blow on the head, and the latter fell and injured his arm severely. The man got away, but was tracked to the Wishing steps, by feathers dropped from his burden. It was afterwards discovered that the fowlhouse at the Deanery, which is near the tower mentioned, had been broken into, and a number of hens stolen from it. On Thursday night, Detective-sergeants Wallace and Nixon arrested the prisoner Snarps, who was identified by Snaith as the assailant. bliarpe was remanded.

A very shocking illustration of the penalties attach- ng to the excessive use of stimulants has been at. forded in connection with the proceedings of a Liver- pool man, when on a visit for the purpose of spending his Christmas holidays in Widnes. The man's friends live at Lugsdale, and arrived at Widnes on Saturday. He appears to have consumed spirits to an enormous extent, and to have provided himself with bottles of rum, which were concealed about his person to deceive the household; and in the end, and when his flionds were temporarily absent from the house, he suddenly lost consciousness, and fell with consider- able- violence in the grate. One of the bottles of rum was broken in the fall, and the contents spread- ing in and around the grate, the inebriate won became enveloped in dames. He appears speedily to have become aware of the perilous position in veLiia he was placed, for rushing into the yard, ho shrieked piteously for assistance, and a constable was thus drawn to the spot. With difficulty his clothes were removed, and then it was found that the man bad been shockingly burnt, although he fortunately uacap ed with his life.

THE BOWDON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. We are informed that the Rev. Alex. Mackennal, 8.A., of Leicester, has accepted a hearty and unani- mous invitation to the pastorate of the Bowdon Con- gregational Church, and that his ministry there will commence on the fiat Sunday in February.

GREAT BILLIARD MATCH AT MANCHESTER. On Monday evening a billiard match, between Mr. John Roberts, sea., ex-champion of England, and Mr. W. Harrison, a Manchester player of some note, took place at the Old Griffin Inn, GFosvenor-strest, Man- chester. The comfort of the visitors was of a most luxuriant character, and at the conclusion of the game the numbers were declared, Roberts 750, Harrison 600. Roberts gave his opponent 200 points. The break of the evening was made by Roberts, who scored 86, which included 20 spot strokes, The ex-champion drew up to his opponent at 493, after which the pros- pects of Mr. Harrison were not bright. Oat of five games at pyramids Mr, Harrison won three and Mr. Roberts two. .
